extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, district court judges, patent practitioners, and parties in U.S. patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether asserted patent claims satisfy 35 U.S.C. § 101 (the Alice/Mayo two-step test), typically at the Rule 12(b)(6) pleadings stage; includes when claim construction is or is not required and whether amendment would be futile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 12(b)(6) pleading standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss, the court must accept as true all factual allegations in the complaint and view them in the light most favorable to the plaintiff; dismissal is appropriate only if the complaint does not contain sufficient factual matter to state a claim plausible on its face (Iqbal/Twombly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court need not accept as true allegations that contradict matters properly subject to judicial notice or exhibits, such as the claims and patent specification (Secured Mail Solutions). Patent eligibility can be resolved at the pleading stage when no factual allegations prevent resolving the eligibility question as a matter of law (Aatrix Software).

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 as a threshold legal issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 is a threshold test and may be decided early in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because §101 is a threshold inquiry, courts may decide eligibility at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage when the patent and complaint show ineligibility (Bilski; Cleveland Clinic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory scope of patent-eligible subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101 allows patents for any new and useful 'process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court recognizes judicial exceptions—laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas—that are not patentable (Alice; Mayo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: First determine whether the claims are drawn to a patent-ineligible concept; if so, look to the elements of the claim individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether there is an 'inventive concept' sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the ineligible concept (Alice/Mayo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At step one courts ask what the claim is 'directed to'; at step two courts examine whether additional features are more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity (Ultramercial; BSG Tech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizing the claim 'directed to' focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The court should identify whether the claim is truly focused on an abstract idea (or other ineligible matter) by reference to the claim language; the specification may help but must yield to the claim language in identifying the focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim language defines the breadth of the claim and thus the preemption concern; reliance on the specification cannot override what the claims actually claim (ChargePoint; Alice; Graver Tank).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern as the basis for exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial exceptions to patentability are driven by the concern of preemption—preventing patenting that would monopolize basic tools of scientific and technological work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess whether the claim would preempt all applications of the underlying idea; broad claims that effectively cover an entire field are problematic (Alice; Mayo; ChargePoint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement (Alice step two)
rubrics_metrics.description: To transform an unpatentable law of nature or abstract idea into a patent-eligible application, the claim must include an inventive concept—an element or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the patent is significantly more than the ineligible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventive concept must be more than a drafting effort or the application of the abstract idea using conventional and well-understood techniques; generic or conventional components do not qualify (Alice; Ultramercial; BSG Tech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional components do not supply inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely add conventional elements or generic physical limitations (e.g., 'upper layer,' 'lower layer,' conventional processors) to an abstract idea fail to supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification describes components as 'conventional' or 'generally available,' that supports a finding that the claim elements are routine and not inventive (numerous specification citations; TLI; Ariosa; Mayo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/apparatus claims can still be abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to physical devices are not immune from §101 scrutiny; a claim reciting concrete, tangible components can nonetheless be directed to an abstract idea if those components merely provide a generic environment for the abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include apparatus claims found abstract where physical limitations simply describe a conventional environment (ChargePoint; TLI). Courts look to whether the asserted improvement is a specific technical improvement or merely the abstract idea implemented in a physical setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enfish distinction (improvement vs. abstract idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relevant inquiry is whether the claims are directed to an improvement in technology/functionality (which may be patent eligible) versus being directed to an abstract idea implemented with conventional components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim outlines a specific asserted improvement to computer (or other) functionality it may not be abstract (Enfish). By contrast, merely applying a sensor at the nanoscale without a technical improvement is not an 'Enfish' style inventive focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precedent and comparing to prior cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts generally seek to compare the claims at issue to claims previously found to be directed to abstract ideas to navigate the boundaries of the abstract-idea category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categories that have been recognized as abstract include fundamental economic practices, methods of organizing human activity, and mathematical algorithms; courts use decisions such as Bilski, Benson, Alice, Enfish, TLI, Ariosa, ChargePoint, Solutran for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative claim approach
rubrics_metrics.description: A court need not individually address every claim if a representative claim is identified and all claims are substantially similar and linked to the same abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content Extraction permits use of a representative claim when claims are substantially similar; the court must ensure the representative claim accurately captures the focus of the asserted claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction not always required for §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is not an inviolable prerequisite to a §101 determination when eligibility is apparent from the face of the patent and complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genetic Technologies and other Federal Circuit authority permit §101 rulings without full claim construction where resolution can be made as a matter of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification can confirm conventionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in the specification that components or fabrication are 'conventional' or 'well-known' support the conclusion that claim elements are routine and do not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will point to specification language describing self-assembled monolayers, field-effect transistors, conventional semiconductor processes, conventional driver circuits, or conventional readout methods as evidence that the claimed elements are not inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Futility of amendment / leave to amend standard
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification and claims make clear that the asserted claims are directed to an abstract idea and recite only conventional components, the plaintiff cannot amend to state a valid §101 claim and leave to amend may be denied as futile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the patent itself forecloses any non-abstract formulation of the claims, amendment is futile (citing Shane v. Fauver and the court's reasoning here).
